title: Subscriptions to GLAD deforestation alerts lower the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18%
summary: Four researchers, two of them from the operator and the producer of the alerts, found that subscriptions to GLAD Landsat alerts cut the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18%.
account: Global Forest Watch's GLAD deforestation alerts are produced by the University of Maryland from Landsat imagery. Bagged decision trees estimate the per-pixel likelihood of forest loss. The method was published on 2 March 2016. Moffette, Alix-Garcia, Shea and Pickens evaluated the alerts' effect in Nature Climate Change on 4 January 2021, analyzing subscriptions to alerts across 22 tropical countries. They found that subscriptions decreased the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18 percent relative to 2011–2016 baseline levels. Effects were stronger in protected areas and concessions. There was no detectable effect on other continents, and little effect where alerts existed without subscribers. They valued the avoided emissions at USD 149–696 million. Two of the study's four authors worked for the operator and the producer of the alerts: Katherine Shea at the World Resources Institute and Amy Pickens at the University of Maryland. The World Resources Institute funded the work. Oregon State University said that the study compared 2011 to 2018, the five years before GLAD launched in 2016 and the first two years after. In a separate randomized trial in the Peruvian Amazon, published in PNAS in July 2021, independent researchers estimated that a community monitoring program built on such alerts cut first-year tree cover loss by 52 percent, an imprecise estimate. Global Forest Watch kept the Landsat-based GLAD alerts running and in 2022 folded them into an integrated layer of disturbance alerts with GLAD-S2 and RADD. On 13 January 2026 Global Forest Watch announced that DIST-ALERT had joined the layer.
purpose: Detect humid tropical forest disturbance in near real time from Landsat imagery to support land management and enforcement.
system: GLAD (Global Land Analysis and Discovery) Landsat deforestation alerts on Global Forest Watch
developer: University of Maryland GLAD laboratory (Hansen et al.)
deployer: World Resources Institute (Global Forest Watch) and alert subscribers

ratings.reason: The study measured an aggregate statistical effect across subscribed areas, and no discrete event can be attributed to a person.
The study measured the effect at the level of subscribed administrative areas and concessions.

The study measured an 18 percent drop in the probability of deforestation in African areas with subscribers, compared with 2011 to 2016 levels. That is a measured improvement in a result. The authors priced the avoided emissions as an estimate, and they found no effect on other continents.

ai_role.statement: The alerts are a machine-learning product (bagged decision trees). The evaluation attributes the 18 percent reduction to subscriptions to those alerts rather than to their mere availability. The evaluation's lead authors are independent economists, but co-authors are from WRI (operator) and the University of Maryland (producer).

fields.summary: Four researchers, two of them from the operator and the producer of the alerts, found that subscriptions to GLAD Landsat alerts cut the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18%.
fields.account: Global Forest Watch's GLAD deforestation alerts are produced by the University of Maryland from Landsat imagery. Bagged decision trees estimate the per-pixel likelihood of forest loss. The method was published on 2 March 2016. Moffette, Alix-Garcia, Shea and Pickens evaluated the alerts' effect in Nature Climate Change on 4 January 2021, analyzing subscriptions to alerts across 22 tropical countries. They found that subscriptions decreased the probability of deforestation in Africa by 18 percent relative to 2011–2016 baseline levels. Effects were stronger in protected areas and concessions. There was no detectable effect on other continents, and little effect where alerts existed without subscribers. They valued the avoided emissions at USD 149–696 million. Two of the study's four authors worked for the operator and the producer of the alerts: Katherine Shea at the World Resources Institute and Amy Pickens at the University of Maryland. The World Resources Institute funded the work. Oregon State University said that the study compared 2011 to 2018, the five years before GLAD launched in 2016 and the first two years after. In a separate randomized trial in the Peruvian Amazon, published in PNAS in July 2021, independent researchers estimated that a community monitoring program built on such alerts cut first-year tree cover loss by 52 percent, an imprecise estimate. Global Forest Watch kept the Landsat-based GLAD alerts running and in 2022 folded them into an integrated layer of disturbance alerts with GLAD-S2 and RADD. On 13 January 2026 Global Forest Watch announced that DIST-ALERT had joined the layer.
